items.title: Obligations under CERT-In and DPDP – Not a zero-sum game
items.summary: India is on the brink of a pivotal moment in its data privacy landscape - one that will reshape not only regulatory practice but also the everyday interaction of individuals and businesses with digital ecosystems. With the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (‘DPDP Act’) and its accompanying Rules (‘DPDP Rules’) poised for implementation, the task of integrating this new framework within the existing regulatory regime assumes critical importance. The central issue is whether the DPDP regime will operate in harmony with parallel obligations or whether it risks creating conflicting compliance tracks. The DPDP Act has largely sought to avoid potential conflicts with the erstwhile regulatory framework governing data privacy through the repeal of relevant provisions and rules of the Information Technology Act. A significant exception, however, is the 2022 directions issued by the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (‘CERT-In’) under Section 70-B(6) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (‘CERT-In Directions’), which continue to survive. items.title: Kerala HC orders dignified burial of Indian whose body remained in UAE for 18 months amid family dispute
items.summary: The Kerala High Court recently stepped in to ensure the dignified burial of a 71-year-old Indian man who died in March 2025 in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and whose body remained there due to a dispute between his relatives as to where he should be buried [ Mary Victoria v Ministry of External Affairs & ors ]. Justice PV Kunhikrishnan passed the order after observing that disputed between the deceased man's relatives as to whether he should be buried in India at the family tomb or abroad cannot indefinitely prolong his burial. The Court further emphasised that every person deserves a dignified burial regardless of their financial or social status. Ensuring a decent burial is the responsibility of relatives, society, and ultimately the State, if the others fail to fulfil that duty, the Court said. items.title: Choosing your counsel in the Supreme Court: Why strategy matters more than a big name
items.summary: In litigation, we often hear "facts win cases." After years of managing litigation, I have realised that in the Supreme Court, facts alone do not win cases; strategy does. And the most critical part of that strategy is choosing the right arguing counsel. I want to share a recent experience that taught me this lesson the hard way. Journey of a case We lost at every stage. The statutory appeal was dismissed. The statutory revision failed. The writ petition was not entertained. With little hope left, we filed a letters patent appeal (LPA) before the Division Bench. This time, we engaged a non-senior counsel who had actually read our brief threadbare. She knew the record. She persuaded the Division Bench not by rhetoric, but by methodical presentation. We won. The Division Bench reversed all the earlier findings. That victory brought us to the Supreme Court - the last forum for justice - as the opposite side challenged the Division Bench order. items.title: Lawyers submitting fake affidavits spoil the faith of Bar-friendly judges: Kerala High Court
items.summary: Kerala High Court judge Justice Kauser Edappagath on Friday revealed in open court that there have been several instances of advocates filing fake affidavits. The day of hearings was drawing to a close when the judge, who was hearing bail matters all day, was confronted with a case where the counsel representing the accused sought relief on the ground that a settlement had been reached with the complainant. Justice Edappagath said that he cannot accept such submissions or affidavits on blind faith without giving the prosecution time to get instructions and verify its authenticity. " There have been so many cases where affidavits are filed and when later the prosecutor is asked to get instructions, it turns out they are fake. Just ask the prosecutor ," Justice Edappagath orally remarked. The judge also questioned why lawyers seem to work under the impression that the court can grant bail or any other relief on a plea moved mere hours earlier, without giving a chance for the State prosecutor to get instructions on the matter. items.title: High Court can order restoration of electricity in disputes involving power theft: Supreme Court
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday held that High Courts can order the restoration of electricity supply that was disconnected over disputed allegations of theft, but advised against adopting a liberal approach in such cases [ Dakshin Gujarat Vij Vs Vaibhav Crusher ]. A Bench of Justices Manoj Misra and KV Viswanathan observed that electricity is essential for life and livelihood, and that its deprivation could have serious consequences. Therefore, constitutional courts can intervene to protect consumers against arbitrary disruption of electricity supply by electricity distribution companies, it held. " Electricity is an essential commodity necessary for both life and livelihood. Its deprivation may have serious consequences. In an appropriate case, the High Court may be justified in exercising its constitutional powers to protect a person from an arbitrary action of the State and its instrumentalities including a distribution licensee, " the judgment stated. The Court, however, cautioned that a liberal approach may not be appropriate in cases involving allegations of electricity theft. A coram of Commission President Justice Sangita Dhingra Sehgal and Member Bimla Kumari found that the bank had failed to establish that the locker was surrendered or that its contents were returned to the complainant. It held, " Further, there is no receipt of the items in the locker of the Complainant and her deceased father-in-law provided by the Opposite Party at the time of the alleged surrender of the said locker, hence, it is clear that the belongings of the Complainant were misappropriated by the Opposite Party, and that the Complainant had never surrendered her locker facility ." The joint locker was maintained by Monica Marwah and her father-in-law since 1998 at Union Bank's Naraina Vihar branch in Delhi. items.summary: The Additional District Judge whose his son was recently involved in a car crash that killed a scooter rider, has moved the Kerala High Court seeking anticipatory bail. The petition is listed for hearing today before Justice Kauser Edappagath . The accused-judge's 17-year-old son was driving a Mercedes-Benz car when he hit a two-wheeler in Kochi's Cheranalloor on October 25, killing the scooter rider, one Jayabalakrishnan. The judge who is posted at a Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) at Iranjalakuda in Thrissur district, has been arraigned as an accused in the FIR registered by the Police after the crash. Section 199A provides that when a minor commits a motor vehicle offence, the guardian or vehicle owner is presumed to be responsible and can be prosecuted and punished, subject to statutory exceptions.
